schema.name: Workflow
schema.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. The cache is positional: agent() calls replay from cache up to the first call that failed, no longer matches the earlier run (edited, added, removed or reordered) or never started in it; that call and every call after it run again, even when their own (prompt, opts) are unchanged. A call a usage limit refused, or one still running when the run stopped, usually runs again without ending reuse: finished calls after it still come from cache. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

# The Pre-flight Scan

Part of superpowers:subagent-driven-development. Run it once, before
dispatching Task 1.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts, writing down
what you checked as you check it:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

The scan's output is a table, not a verdict. One row for every pair of tasks
that share a file or an interface: the two tasks, what one produces against
what the other consumes, and what you found. One row for every task: whether
its own text agrees with itself — the tests it specifies against the code it
specifies, the files it creates against the files it later touches. "The scan
is clean" without those rows is not a scan you ran.

Write the table to the ledger. Rule on everything you find before execution
begins — each finding against the plan text that mandates it — and record
each ruling in the ledger. If the scan is clean, proceed without comment.
Rule on each conflict it surfaces — the spec is the binding authority, the
plan is its argument — record the ruling beside its row, and dispatch
Task 1. The review loop remains the net for conflicts that only emerge from
implementation.
# Implementer Subagent Prompt Template

Use this template when dispatching an implementer subagent.

```
Subagent (general-purpose):
  description: "Implement Task N: [task name]"
  model: [MODEL — REQUIRED: choose per SKILL.md Model Selection; an omitted
         model silently inherits the session's most expensive one]
  prompt: |
    You are implementing Task N: [task name]

    ## Task Description

    Read your task brief first: [BRIEF_FILE]
    It contains the full task text from the plan.

    ## Context

    [Scene-setting: where this fits, dependencies, architectural context]

    ## Before You Begin

    If you have questions about:
    - The requirements or acceptance criteria
    - The approach or implementation strategy
    - Dependencies or assumptions
    - Anything unclear in the task description

    **Ask them now.** Raise any concerns before starting work.

    ## Your Job

    Once you're clear on requirements:
    1. Implement exactly what the task specifies
    2. Write tests (following TDD if task says to)
    3. Verify implementation works
    4. Commit your work
    5. Self-review (see below)
    6. Report back

    Work from: [directory]

    **While you work:** If you encounter something unexpected or unclear, **ask questions**.
    It's always OK to pause and clarify. Don't guess or make assumptions.

    While iterating, run the focused test for what you're changing; run the
    full suite once before committing, not after every edit.

    ## You Do Not Dispatch Subagents

    Do all of this task's work yourself. Never spawn a subagent to
    implement part of the task, and above all never spawn a reviewer to
    check your work. Self-review (below) means reading your own diff.
    Review is the controller's job: after you report, it dispatches a
    fresh reviewer against your diff. A reviewer you spawn duplicates
    that review at full cost, and its approval counts for nothing in
    the process. If you catch yourself thinking "an independent review
    would strengthen my report" — that review is already scheduled.
    Report instead.

    ## Code Organization

    You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more
    reliable when files are focused. Keep this in mind:
    - Follow the file structure defined in the plan
    - Each file should have one clear responsibility with a well-defined interface
    - If a file you're creating is growing beyond the plan's intent, stop and report
      it as DONE_WITH_CONCERNS — don't split files on your own without plan guidance
    - If an existing file you're modifying is already large or tangled, work carefully
      and note it as a concern in your report
    - In existing codebases, follow established patterns. Improve code you're touching
      the way a good developer would, but don't restructure things outside your task.

    ## When You're in Over Your Head

    It is always OK to stop and say "this is too hard for me." Bad work is worse than
    no work. You will not be penalized for escalating.

    **STOP and escalate when:**
    - The task requires architectural decisions with multiple valid approaches
    - You need to understand code beyond what was provided and can't find clarity
    - You feel uncertain about whether your approach is correct
    - The task involves restructuring existing code in ways the plan didn't anticipate
    - You've been reading file after file trying to understand the system without progress

    **How to escalate:** Report back with status BLOCKED or NEEDS_CONTEXT. Describe
    specifically what you're stuck on, what you've tried, and what kind of help you need.
    The controller can provide more context, re-dispatch with a more capable model,
    or break the task into smaller pieces.

    ## Before Reporting Back: Self-Review

    Review your work with fresh eyes. Ask yourself:

    **Completeness:**
    - Did I fully implement everything in the spec?
    - Did I miss any requirements?
    - Are there edge cases I didn't handle?

    **Quality:**
    - Is this my best work?
    - Are names clear and accurate (match what things do, not how they work)?
    - Is the code clean and maintainable?

    **Discipline:**
    - Did I avoid overbuilding (YAGNI)?
    - Did I only build what was requested?
    - Did I follow existing patterns in the codebase?

    **Testing:**
    - Do tests actually verify behavior (not just mock behavior)?
    - Did I follow TDD if required?
    - Are tests comprehensive?
    - Is the test output pristine (no stray warnings or noise)?

    If you find issues during self-review, fix them now before reporting.

    ## After Review Findings

    If the task review finds issues, you will be resumed with the findings.
    Fix them, re-run the tests that cover the amended code, and append a fix
    report to your report file: what you changed, the covering tests you
    ran, the command, and the output. Reviewers will not re-run tests for
    you — your report is the test evidence. Then reply with the same short
    status contract as your first report.

    ## Report Format

    Write your full report to [REPORT_FILE]:
    - What you implemented (or what you attempted, if blocked)
    - What you tested and test results
    - **TDD Evidence** (if TDD was required for this task):
      - RED: command run, relevant failing output before implementation, and why the failure was expected
      - GREEN: command run and relevant passing output after implementation
    - Files changed
    - Self-review findings (if any)
    - Any issues or concerns

    Then report back with ONLY (under 15 lines — the detail lives in the
    report file):
    - **Status:** DONE | DONE_WITH_CONCERNS | BLOCKED | NEEDS_CONTEXT
    - Commits created (short SHA + subject)
    - One-line test summary (e.g. "14/14 passing, output pristine")
    - Your concerns, if any
    - The report file path

    If BLOCKED or NEEDS_CONTEXT, put the specifics in the final message
    itself — the controller acts on it directly.

    Use DONE_WITH_CONCERNS if you completed the work but have doubts about correctness.
    Use BLOCKED if you cannot complete the task. Use NEEDS_CONTEXT if you need
    information that wasn't provided. Never silently produce work you're unsure about.
```

# SMA-804 Turn-Boundary Checkpoint Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Add an optional `TurnCheckpoint` callback on `RunContext`. The `LlmAgent` loop calls it between turns, and it can continue the run, inject user content, or stop the run cleanly.

**Architecture:** A new `checkpoint` module in `paigasus-helikon-core` defines the trait and its types. The `LlmAgent::run` driver (`core/src/agent.rs`) detects the boundary batch from `transition()`, which is `ExecutingTools` followed by `CallModel`. It calls the callback before it handles `TurnStarted { n }`. `transition()` does not change. Two new `AgentEvent` variants carry the result: `UserMessageInjected` (not terminal) and `RunStopped` (terminal). Phase B connects `RunStopped` to SMA-803's `StopReason`.

**Tech Stack:** Rust 1.94, `async_trait`, `async_stream`, `tokio`, `insta` snapshots, `tracing`.

**Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-18-sma-804-turn-boundary-checkpoint-design.md`. Read it with this plan. The section numbers below (§5.3 and others) refer to it.

## Global Constraints

- Work in the worktree `/Users/smaschek/dev/paigasus/paigasus-helikon/.claude/worktrees/sma-804-turn-boundary-checkpoint`, on the branch `feature/sma-804-turn-boundary-checkpoint-a-runcontext`. Use worktree-absolute paths for every Write and Edit.
- Do not run `git checkout`, `git switch`, `git reset`, `git rebase` or `git stash` unless a task tells you to. Another session (SMA-803) works in a sibling worktree.
- Run every cargo command in the foreground, and wait for it to finish. Do not end your turn while a command runs.
- Commit format: `<type>(<scope>): SMA-804 <lowercase verb> …`, with the trailer `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Use the scopes `core`, `runtime`, `docs`. Run `cargo fmt --all` before each commit.
- **No hand version bumps.** Every touched crate is already released, so release-plz bumps core and the dependents in one release PR (pure-auto, proven in SMA-418 / PR #80). Do not edit any `version =` or CHANGELOG.
- All new public types are `#[non_exhaustive]`. No existing variant gets a new field (G6).
- Every new public item has a `///` doc. Public docs must not intra-doc-link to `pub(crate)` items (`Interceptors`, `user_text_of`), or the `docs` gate fails.
- New insta snapshots are committed as `.snap` files. Do not leave `.snap.new` files.
- Tracing targets follow the `paigasus::core::agent` pattern. The `tests/workspace-lints` tracing-target check must pass.

## Review Focus

These failure modes follow from the spec, but no spec test covers them. Each one has a test in the task that owns the code:

1. **Parallel tool calls in one turn.** The checkpoint runs exactly once, after *both* results (Task 3, `checkpoint_runs_once_after_parallel_results`).
2. **An `Inject` with only an image part.** The guardrails get `""` and pass, and the image is recorded and sent (Task 3, `inject_image_only_passes_guardrails_and_is_sent`).
3. **Several boundaries in one run.** An `Inject` at boundary 1 and a `Stop` at boundary 2. The second request holds the first injection, the second `TurnBoundary` has `completed_turn = 1`, and `usage` covers three model calls (Task 4, `inject_then_stop_across_two_boundaries`).
4. **A run with no tool calls.** The checkpoint is never called (Task 3, `checkpoint_not_called_without_tool_calls`).
5. **An `Inject` inside a handoff child.** The recorder stores it after the child's `ToolReturned`, and the parent's history order stays valid (Task 4, `handoff_child_inject_is_recorded_in_order`).

---

### Task 7: Other runtimes: clear and warn, explicit arms, Temporal note

**Files:**
- Modify, to clear and warn (one private helper per crate, `fn restrict_unsupported_run_features<Ctx>(ctx: RunContext<Ctx>) -> RunContext<Ctx>`, called directly after each `state.context.build(..)`). SMA-803 creates a helper with this exact name and signature for its deferral flag. If SMA-803 is already on `main`, add the checkpoint clear inside the existing helper, and do not add a second call. If it is not, create the helper with only the checkpoint clear. At the Task 9 rebase, merge the two bodies into one helper with one call per site:
  - `crates/paigasus-helikon-runtime-axum/src/handlers/runs.rs:220` (helper in `src/context.rs`, doc on `ContextProvider` at `:71`)
  - `crates/paigasus-helikon-runtime-actix/src/handlers/runs.rs:257` (helper in `src/context.rs`, doc on `ContextProvider` at `:86`)
  - `crates/paigasus-helikon-runtime-agentcore/src/invoke.rs:165`, `ws.rs:203`, `agui/sse.rs:147`, `agui/ws.rs:267`, `a2a/rpc.rs:519` (one helper in the crate, for example in `src/error.rs` or a new `src/checkpoint.rs`)
- Modify, for explicit event arms where the event has a meaning: `runtime-agentcore/src/agui/map.rs` (`helikon.user_message_injected`, `helikon.run_stopped` CUSTOM frames), `cli/src/repl.rs` (print both events), `evals/src/evaluators/trajectory.rs`, `paigasus-helikon-mcp/src/server.rs`, and the axum/actix `dto.rs`, `event_log.rs`, `registry.rs`. In each file, decide whether the existing wildcard is correct. Add an arm only where the event changes the output. Write the result for each file in the commit body.
- Modify: `crates/paigasus-helikon-runtime-temporal/src/runner.rs:~184`. Add `tracing::warn!` when `ctx.turn_checkpoint().is_some()`, and a doc note on `TemporalRunner`.

For the checkpoint, the helper logs `tracing::warn!(target: "paigasus::runtime::<crate>", "turn checkpoint is not supported by this runtime; ignored")` and returns `ctx.without_turn_checkpoint()`. It logs only when a checkpoint was set. Match each crate's existing tracing-target style.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing tests.** In each of axum, actix and agentcore, write `context_provider_checkpoint_never_fires`. A test `ContextProvider` sets a counting checkpoint, and the agent makes one tool turn over the crate's run endpoint. Use the crate's existing handler-test harness. The counter is 0, and the run status is `Completed`.
- [ ] **Step 2: Run the tests and confirm they fail.** Command: `cargo test -p paigasus-helikon-runtime-axum -p paigasus-helikon-runtime-actix -p paigasus-helikon-runtime-agentcore context_provider_checkpoint_never_fires`. Expected: FAIL (the counter is 1).
- [ ] **Step 3: Implement** the helpers, the calls, the docs, the arms and the Temporal warning.
- [ ] **Step 4: Run the tests and confirm they pass.** Commands: the command from Step 2, then `cargo test --workspace --all-features`.
- [ ] **Step 5: Commit.** Message: `feat(runtime): SMA-804 ignore the turn checkpoint in http and temporal runtimes`.

### Task 8: Provider wire check and documentation

**Files:**
- Test: the request translators of `providers-gemini` (`src/translate/request.rs:41-80`), `providers-anthropic`, `providers-openai` (chat and responses) and `providers-bedrock`. Add one unit test per translator.
- Modify: `docs/book/src/concepts/agent-loop.md`
- Check: `crates/paigasus-helikon-core/README.md`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the translator tests.** The test `tool_result_then_user_message_request_shape` builds `[UserMessage, AssistantMessage, ToolCall, ToolResult, UserMessage([Text "news"])]` and checks the exact wire JSON. For Gemini, assert the current shape. Then compare it with the Gemini API rules for consecutive `user` contents (the Gemini API docs, or a keyless container proxy if one is available). If the API rejects it, merge the parts in the translator and state the source in the commit body. Also add `empty_text_part_is_dropped_or_rejected` for the Anthropic translator. If neither happens, report it. Do not change the behaviour without a source.
- [ ] **Step 2: Run the tests.** Command: `cargo test -p paigasus-helikon-providers-gemini -p paigasus-helikon-providers-anthropic -p paigasus-helikon-providers-openai -p paigasus-helikon-providers-bedrock tool_result_then_user_message`.
- [ ] **Step 3: Update the book.** Add `UserMessageInjected` and `RunStopped` to the event list in `agent-loop.md` (lines 56-66). Add the section "Turn-boundary checkpoint", with the content listed in spec §6.4, and a short Rust example that uses `ScriptedCheckpoint`-style code: a struct that implements `TurnCheckpoint<()>`. Add a line to the core README only if the README lists `RunContext` features.
- [ ] **Step 4: Verify.** Command: `mdbook build docs/book` (clean, linkcheck on). Then `npx markdownlint-cli2`.
- [ ] **Step 5: Commit.** Use `test(providers): SMA-804 pin the tool-result then user-message wire shape` and `docs(book): SMA-804 document the turn-boundary checkpoint` as separate commits.

- Consumes: Tasks 1-3.
- Produces: the run ends with `RunStopped { reason, usage }` and then `OnRunComplete`. Phase B (Task 9) maps this to `StopReason`.

**Mechanism.**
- On `Stop { reason }`, or on a guardrail tripwire for injected content:
  1. On a tripwire, first yield `GuardrailTriggered { kind, info }`, and use `reason = "input guardrail tripwire"`.
  2. Take `usage` from the `ExecutingTools { usage, .. }` state before the transition.
  3. Record `gen_ai.usage.*` on `run_span`, and record the stop reason (attribute `paigasus.stop_reason`). Do not set `otel.status_code = ERROR`.
  4. Yield `RunStopped { reason, usage }`.
  5. Set `next_action = NextAction::Terminate`, and `break` out of the event loop, so that `TurnStarted { n }` is not handled or yielded.
  6. The existing `Terminate` arm then fires `OnRunComplete`. `loop_state` is not `Failed`, so the `FailureSlot` stays empty.
- Handoff re-yield: add the arm `RunStopped { reason, usage }`. It adds `parent_usage`, records the span usage, and yields `RunStopped { reason, usage: total }`. This is the same as the `RunCompleted` arm.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing tests.**
  - `stop_ends_cleanly_at_boundary`: `[Stop { "operator" }]`. The last event is `RunStopped { reason: "operator", usage }`, with `usage` equal to turn 0's usage. There is no `TurnStarted { 1 }` and no `RunFailed`. The model was called once. `with_failure(..).collect()` is `Ok`, and the slot is empty. A recording hook sees `OnRunComplete` exactly once. A `SessionRecorder` over the events gives a `ToolReturned` for every `ToolCalled`.
  - `guardrail_tripwire_on_injection_stops`: a guardrail that trips on the text "bad". With `[Inject([Text "bad"])]`, the event order ends with `GuardrailTriggered`, `RunStopped { reason: "input guardrail tripwire", .. }`. There is no `UserMessageInjected`. The model was called once, and the recorder output has no `UserMessage` with "bad".
  - `guardrail_error_on_injection_stops`: a guardrail that returns `Err` gives the same result as the previous test.
  - `handoff_child_stop_ends_whole_run`: a parent that hands off to a child. The child makes one tool turn, and then the checkpoint (inherited) returns `Stop`. The boundary is `TurnBoundary::new(0, 1, "child", 1)`. The last event is `RunStopped`, with `usage` equal to the parent's usage plus the child's usage. This test does not check the pairing of `ToolCalled` (SMA-810).
  - Review Focus 3, `inject_then_stop_across_two_boundaries`: three scripted model turns (tool, tool, text) and `[Inject([Text "a"]), Stop { "b" }]`. Request #2 holds the `UserMessage("a")`. `boundaries()[1].completed_turn == 1`. `RunStopped.usage` covers two model calls.
  - Review Focus 5, `handoff_child_inject_is_recorded_in_order`: the child gets `Inject([Text "x"])`. In the recorder output, the `UserMessage("x")` comes directly after the child's `ToolReturned`.

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement the mechanism above.**
- [ ] **Step 4: Run the tests and confirm they pass.** Command: `cargo test -p paigasus-helikon-core`.
- [ ] **Step 5: Commit.** Message: `feat(core): SMA-804 stop the run cleanly at a turn boundary`.

  - I did not run the suite.

content.content:
# The Fix Loop

Part of superpowers:subagent-driven-development. The task review reported
spec ❌, a Critical or Important finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real
gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is yours to rule on: weigh the finding
  against the plan text, decide with the spec as the binding authority, and
  ledger the ruling before you act on it. Do not dismiss the finding because
  the plan mandates it, and do not dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan
  without a recorded ruling.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
SKILL.md's Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
by its absolute path, from the working tree you're executing in, where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](../re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — Ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: rule on the smallest change that unblocks the dependent work,
  ledger it as `Task <N>: Ruling: <finding> — <what you decided and why>`,
  and carry it into the next task's dispatch. Parking a structural failure
  silently lets every dependent task build on it. Stop only when the defect
  leaves every path forward a guess.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

Task 4 review: fix round 1. One Important finding, verbatim from the reviewer:

"Important. The `ToolReturned` assertion in `stop_ends_cleanly_at_boundary` (test diff :277-287) cannot fail. `SessionRecorder::drain` (session.rs:523-547) adds a synthetic `ToolReturned` for every `ToolCalled` that has no result. So `called == returned` is always true after `drain()`. Example: a later change to the stop path skips a `ToolOutputItem`. This test still passes. The fix is to count `ToolOutputItem` against `ToolCallItem` in the raw `out.events`. Another fix is to assert that no `ToolReturned` holds the text \"tool call did not complete\"."

Do both: count ToolOutputItem vs ToolCallItem in the raw events, and assert that no recorded ToolReturned is the synthetic one (check the exact synthetic text in session.rs). Mutation-check it: temporarily make the assertion face a missing result (e.g. drop one ToolOutputItem from the event vec in the test) and confirm it fails, then revert that test-only mutation. Production code stays unchanged.

Same hard rules as before (foreground, no HEAD-moving git, worktree-absolute paths, explicit git add, fmt, trailer). Commit as `test(core): SMA-804 make the stop test detect a missing tool result`. Run `cargo test -p paigasus-helikon-core --test turn_checkpoint`.   2. Findings
  - Critical: none.
  - Important: none.
  - Minor: none that need a change. Two notes follow, both non-blocking.
    - turn_checkpoint.rs:322 (risk 1). The `!events.iter().any(is_injected)` check does bite, even though the implementer's mutation did not reach it.
      - It reads `session.events(None)`. That is the persisted store, and the same store the production recorder writes to.
      - session.rs:511 records `UserMessageInjected` as soon as the event passes `observe`. agent.rs:960 yields that event only after `run_input_guardrails`.
      - If a mutation yielded the event before the hanging guardrail, `observe` would push `UserMessage("news")`. The cancel path calls `finalize` (lib.rs:212 and following), so the message would reach the session. `is_injected` matches exactly `[Text "news"]`, so it would trip.
      - The `tool_returned_count == 1` assertion beside it confirms the turn-0 tool result is kept.
    - Cancel tests (risk 1, minor). The `Cancelled` result assertion is checked first, so under the implementer's mutation that assertion failed before the session check ran. This is only a diagnostic ordering effect. Each assertion is independent and neither is vacuous.

  - Risk 3 (event order). The persistence test asserts UserMessage, ToolCalled, ToolReturned, the injected UserMessage and AssistantMessage at indexes 0 to 4, exactly as the brief requires.
  - Risk 4 (streamed stop). The test calls `run_streamed`, drains the stream under a timeout, and asserts the last event is `RunStopped` with reason "enough". It then checks one `ToolReturned` and no injected message in the session. `finalize` runs before the terminal event is yielded (lib.rs:205 to 213), so reading the session right after the stream ends is race-free.

I also did not confirm that `GuardrailInput::UserText("news")` is the exact form the injection path passes. If it were not, the guardrail would never hang and the test would fail on the timeout, so that failure would be loud.
  
  4. Verdict: APPROVED

- One private helper per crate with exact signature `fn restrict_unsupported_run_features<Ctx>(ctx: RunContext<Ctx>) -> RunContext<Ctx>`, called exactly once directly after each `state.context.build(..)`; warns only when a checkpoint was set; text "turn checkpoint is not supported by this runtime; ignored"; tracing target per crate style (`paigasus::runtime::<crate>`). The implementer raised concerns; judge each on the merits:
1. The endpoint tests use scripted agents that read `ctx.turn_checkpoint()` by hand instead of running the real LlmAgent loop. Is that an adequate proof that the checkpoint never fires through the endpoint (the brief says "the agent makes one tool turn ... the counter is 0")? A test that would pass with the helper call removed is Important.
2. In agentcore only `invoke` has a direct test; ws, agui/sse, agui/ws and a2a/rpc call the same helper without tests. Verify by reading that each of those five sites really calls the helper on the built context that is then used for the run (not a copy, not before a later rebuild).
3. axum/actix dto.rs map `RunStopped` to status `Completed` because RunStatus has no stopped value. Since the HTTP runtimes clear the checkpoint, can RunStopped reach these runtimes at all? Is mapping to Completed (vs Failed, or a wildcard) a sound, non-misleading choice, and is it documented? Note RunStatus is likely public API; adding a variant would be a public change outside the brief.
4. AG-UI CUSTOM frames `helikon.user_message_injected` / `helikon.run_stopped`: does RunStopped also emit the terminal RUN_FINISHED frame the protocol needs, so a client does not hang?
5. Event-log / registry: is RunStopped treated as terminal wherever RunCompleted/RunFailed are (run finished, status set, stream closed)?

Read the diff once; one focused check per named risk. Read-only: never mutate the tree, index, HEAD or branches. Do not dispatch subagents. Do not run the suite (one focused test allowed for a concrete doubt).

- `03376131` maps the two new events in the event consumers.

Task 7 passed the Opus review with no Critical or Important findings. The reviewer accepted the three concerns:

- **Scripted agents:** the endpoint tests still fail if the helper call is removed. The core tests already prove that the real agent loop calls the checkpoint.
- **The four agentcore sites with no test:** each site passes the cleared context to the run, and no code rebuilds the context after the helper call.
- **`RunStopped` shown as `Completed`:** this is a sound choice. A `RunStopped` can reach these runtimes only from a custom agent, because the helper clears the checkpoint. A "stopped" status value would change the public API, so it is not in this task.

I wrote the minor findings in the ledger. One is about two old doc comments that name only `RunCompleted` and `RunFailed` as terminal events.

Task 8, the last Phase A task, now runs. It has two parts:
- Each provider translator gets a test that pins how it sends a tool result followed by a user message.
- The book gets a "Turn-boundary checkpoint" section.

If the documentation of a provider says that it rejects this message shape, the implementer only reports it, with the source. I then decide on a translator change. The implementer does not change provider behavior without a cited source.

Task 8 is committed in two parts:
- `2848141d` adds the provider wire tests.
- `493a6944` adds the book section.

**Tests:** the new tests pass in all five translators, and clippy is clean. The mdBook build is clean with linkcheck on. Markdownlint reports 0 issues.

The wire check found two problems that I cannot settle from documentation:

- **Gemini:** after an `Inject`, the translator sends two `role: user` contents one after the other: the function response, then the text. The official Gemini docs do not say whether the API accepts this. Some forum threads report a 400 error for this shape, and their workaround is to merge the two contents. I did not change the translator. A live call to the API would settle the question.
- **Anthropic:** an `Inject` with an empty text part becomes an empty text block. The API schema requires at least one character, so the API probably rejects the request. A normal user message with empty text already does the same, so this behavior is old. The new test pins the current behavior, and the implementer did not change it.

OpenAI chat, OpenAI responses and Bedrock send valid shapes. Anthropic and Bedrock already merge the tool result and the text into one user turn.

I wrote both problems in the ledger as open items for you. A Sonnet reviewer now checks Task 8. After that review, Phase A is complete, and I will give you these two decisions.

# Final Review and Finish

Part of superpowers:subagent-driven-development. Every task in the plan is
complete.

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` by its absolute path,
from the working tree you're executing in (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see SKILL.md's Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` by its absolute path,
from the working tree you're executing in, over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](../re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the fix loop's breaker
(references/fix-loop.md): park with rulings, or rule on the load-bearing
ones and ledger what you decided. Only the four things that stop a running
plan (top of SKILL.md) stop you here. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

### Finish

Before you delete anything, collect every ledger line containing `Ruling:` —
preflight rulings, parked findings, breaker adjudications, all of them — into
your final message under "Rulings I made", in the order you made them, each
with what it costs if wrong. The list is exhaustive: if the ledger holds a
ruling, the list holds it. That list is the only place the decisions you
took on your human partner's behalf reach them — they read it and rework
whatever you got wrong. A ruling that dies with the workspace was a decision
made in secret.

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

Phase A is done. All eight tasks are committed on the branch and each one passed its review. Nothing is pushed yet. Phase B waits for SMA-803 to merge, and SMA-803 is not on `main` yet.

## What Phase A does
- **Core:** a host can now attach a `TurnCheckpoint` to `RunContext`. The agent loop calls it between turns, after the tool results. It can continue, inject user content, or stop the run.
  - Injected content goes through the input guardrails and is saved in the session.
  - A stop ends the run cleanly with `RunStopped`. The run is not marked as an error.
- **Scope:** a handoff child inherits the checkpoint. An `AgentAsTool` sub-run and a workflow sub-agent never call it. Tests prove that each of these leaks would be caught.
- **Runtimes:** axum, actix and agentcore remove the checkpoint and log a warning, through the shared helper `restrict_unsupported_run_features`. Temporal logs a warning. `runtime-tokio` saves and cancels correctly, and tests cover this.
- **Book:** `agent-loop.md` has a new "Turn-boundary checkpoint" section.

All tests pass except `trybuild` in core and macros. Those tests also fail on the commit before Task 1, because the local compiler (rustc 1.99) prints different error text. I will check them on CI.

## Decisions I need from you
1. **Gemini wire shape.** After an `Inject`, the Gemini translator sends two `role: user` contents one after the other: the tool result, then the text. No official source says whether the API accepts this. Some forum threads report a 400 error for it. The other four translators send valid shapes. Your options:
   - (a) I merge the two contents into one in the Gemini translator.
   - (b) You make one real call to the API to check.
   - (c) We open a Linear follow-up and leave the shape as it is.
2. **Anthropic empty text.** `Inject([Text ""])` becomes an empty text block. The API requires at least one character, so it will probably return 400. A normal empty user message already does the same today, so this behavior is old. I can make the injection code drop empty text parts, or open a Linear follow-up.
3. **SMA-803 timing.** I wait for SMA-803 to merge and then rebase (my recommendation). If you do not want to wait, I can add `StopReason` myself (the fallback path).

## Decisions I made
- The HTTP helper contains only the checkpoint clear for now, because SMA-803 is not on `main`. If this is wrong, the cost is a merge conflict at the Task 9 rebase, and Task 9 already handles that.
- The `trybuild` failures (core 5/8, macros 3/12) are old and I did not fix them. I confirmed this on the commit before Task 1. If this is wrong, the CI `test` job goes red, and I will check it at Task 10.
- If the current `collect()` does not handle a stopped run, Phase A does not change `runner.rs`, because SMA-803 owns that file. Today `collect()` returns `Ok` for a stopped run, but with zero usage. If this is wrong, the cost is one test edit, and Task 9 maps the usage.
- The book already describes `StopReason::Stopped` and the stop reason in `collect()`. Neither exists in the code yet. Task 9 adds both before the merge. If this is wrong, I rewrite one paragraph. Task 9 must check that paragraph against the code.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   - The user invoked `/feature-factory:feature-pipeline SMA-804`, the full pipeline:
     - Stage 0 intake.
     - Stage 1 spec (brainstorming).
     - Stage 2 adversarial challenge, then **GATE 1**.
     - Stage 3 plan.
     - Stage 4 implementation (subagent-driven).
     - Stage 5 local coderabbit CLI review (max 2 passes, never blocks).
     - Stage 6 `gh pr create`, linked to Linear.
     - Stage 7 coderabbit-loop (max 5 rounds), then **GATE 2**.
     - Stop at every gate.
   - SMA-804 asks for an optional turn-boundary checkpoint callback on `RunContext`:
     - It returns `Continue | Inject(Vec<ContentPart>) | Stop { reason }`.
     - Inject records the content as a UserMessage. The input guardrails check it, and a tripwire leads to a stop.
     - Stop ends the run cleanly.
     - The checkpoint is never called inside a tool call, in an AgentAsTool sub-run, or at a deferred boundary.
     - The change must be compile-compatible.
     - Done when tests show each case and the change is published to crates.io.
   - The user explicitly asked: "coordinate with the other agents in this repo".
   - The spec is approved at GATE 1. The user then chose subagent-driven execution: "yes go subagent".
   - Global instructions:
     - Write all user-facing text in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English. Use short sentences and the active voice, no idioms, keep articles, and use a maximum of 6 sentences per paragraph.
     - Use subagents whenever possible. Pass `model` explicitly: Explore for searches, Haiku for mechanical work, Sonnet for single-domain analysis, and Opus for adversarial review, plan writing and release work.
     - Use they/them for unknown pronouns.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Rust workspace paigasus-helikon. MSRV is 1.94. Local rustc is 1.99.0 with `rust-toolchain.toml` channel stable.
   - `LlmAgent::run` is an `async_stream` driver over the pure `transition()` in loop_state.rs. `transition()` must not change, because Temporal shares it.
   - Boundary detection:
     - In the `for ev in events` loop, before the driver handles `TurnStarted{n}`, it checks for `loop_state` == `ExecutingTools{turn:t}` and `next_action` == `CallModel`.
     - `TurnStarted` is the last event of that batch.
   - Inject:
     1. Validate the parts. ToolUse, ToolResult or Reasoning fails the run with `AgentError::InvalidInjection{reason}`.
     2. An empty Inject is Continue.
     3. Run the guardrails on the text joined by the `user_text_of` rule.
     4. Yield `UserMessageInjected`.
     5. Push to `conversation` and to `request.messages`.
   - Stop and tripwire:
     - On a tripwire, yield `GuardrailTriggered` first, with reason "input guardrail tripwire".
     - Usage comes from the ExecutingTools state. Record `gen_ai.usage.*` and `paigasus.stop_reason`. Do not set ERROR.
     - Yield `RunStopped{reason,usage}`, then `next_action=Terminate` and `break`. The Terminate arm fires OnRunComplete. The FailureSlot stays empty.
   - The handoff re-yield arm for RunStopped adds parent_usage.
   - Scope:
     - handoff_child inherits the checkpoint.
     - subagent_child clears it.
     - to_tool_context, the AgentAsTool sub_ctx and WorkerPosture::apply never carry it.
   - The HTTP runtimes use a private helper per crate, `restrict_unsupported_run_features<Ctx>(ctx: RunContext<Ctx>) -> RunContext<Ctx>`:
     - It is `pub(crate)`, with `where Ctx: Send + Sync + 'static`.
     - It is called once after each `state.context.build(..)`.
     - When a checkpoint was set, it warns "turn checkpoint is not supported by this runtime; ignored".

# The Fix Loop

Part of superpowers:subagent-driven-development. The task review reported
spec ❌, a Critical or Important finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real
gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is yours to rule on: weigh the finding
  against the plan text, decide with the spec as the binding authority, and
  ledger the ruling before you act on it. Do not dismiss the finding because
  the plan mandates it, and do not dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan
  without a recorded ruling.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
SKILL.md's Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
by its absolute path, from the working tree you're executing in, where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](../re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — Ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: rule on the smallest change that unblocks the dependent work,
  ledger it as `Task <N>: Ruling: <finding> — <what you decided and why>`,
  and carry it into the next task's dispatch. Parking a structural failure
  silently lets every dependent task build on it. Stop only when the defect
  leaves every path forward a guess.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are the four named below, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Rulings, not stalls.** A running plan does not wait on a human. Conflicts,
ambiguities, plan defects, a cap you would have asked to exceed — decide
them. The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger as
`Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. A wrong ruling costs rework your human partner can see and undo; a
session parked on a question costs their whole day and buys nothing.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For those,
stop and ask.

## When to Use

```dot
digraph when_to_use {
    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" [shape=diamond];
    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" -> "executing-plans" [label="yes"];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="no"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (inline):**
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution) instead of one context doing every task
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality) instead of only at the end
- Costs a fresh context per task and per review; inline costs one context plus one final reviewer
- Both run in this session, share the same plan workspace and ledger, and never pause between tasks

## The Process

```dot
digraph process {
    rankdir=TB;

    subgraph cluster_per_task {
        label="Per Task";
        "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Implementer asks questions?" [shape=diamond];
        "Answer questions, provide context" [shape=box];
        "Implementer implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [shape=box];
        "Generate review package, dispatch task reviewer (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Spec ✅ and quality approved?" [shape=diamond];
        "Fix loop: read references/fix-loop.md before every round" [shape=box];
        "Append completion to ledger, mark todo complete" [shape=box];
    }

    "Setup: worktree, ledger check, read plan, pre-flight review" [shape=box];
    "More tasks remain?" [shape=diamond];
    "Final review and finish: read references/final-review.md" [shape=box];
    "Final review clean: delete this plan's workspace" [shape=box];
    "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch" [shape=box style=filled fillcolor=lightgreen];

    "Setup: worktree, ledger check, read plan, pre-flight review" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" -> "Implementer asks questions?";
    "Implementer asks questions?" -> "Answer questions, provide context" [label="yes"];
    "Answer questions, provide context" -> "Implementer implements, tests, commits, self-reviews";
    "Implementer asks questions?" -> "Implementer implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [label="no"];
    "Implementer implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" -> "Generate review package, dispatch task reviewer (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)";
    "Generate review package, dispatch task reviewer (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)" -> "Spec ✅ and quality approved?";
    "Spec ✅ and quality approved?" -> "Append completion to ledger, mark todo complete" [label="yes"];
    "Spec ✅ and quality approved?" -> "Fix loop: read references/fix-loop.md before every round" [label="no"];
    "Fix loop: read references/fix-loop.md before every round" -> "Append completion to ledger, mark todo complete" [label="addressed, or parked at the cap"];
    "Append completion to ledger, mark todo complete" -> "More tasks remain?";
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [label="yes"];
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Final review and finish: read references/final-review.md" [label="no"];
    "Final review and finish: read references/final-review.md" -> "Final review clean: delete this plan's workspace";
    "Final review clean: delete this plan's workspace" -> "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch";
}
```

## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `bash scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` by its absolute path, from the
  working tree you're executing in — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (under `<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If one exists,
  read [references/resuming.md](references/resuming.md) before anything
  else: it says whose ledger it is and where to resume.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
rulings made without one are provisional.

Before dispatching Task 1, read [references/preflight.md](references/preflight.md)
and run the conflict scan it describes. Its table and rulings go in the
ledger.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

**Small same-shape work:** when the plan lists several small edits of the
same kind across files, read [references/batching.md](references/batching.md)
before dispatching them.

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

**Waiting on dispatched subagents:** never poll a wait interface with
short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either.
While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review,
reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own.
When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten
minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one
line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase
any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly
all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost
child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `bash scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` by its absolute path, from the
  working tree you're executing in — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- The dispatch carries the no-subagents contract (it is in the
  implementer template): the implementer never dispatches subagents —
  not helpers, and never a reviewer. Review arrives from you, after the
  report. In real sessions, every reviewer a worker spawned duplicated
  the task review the controller dispatched anyway — a full extra
  review seat per task.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` by its absolute path, from the working tree you're executing in — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**Any other status** (DONE_WITH_CONCERNS, NEEDS_CONTEXT, BLOCKED): read
[references/handling-reports.md](references/handling-reports.md) and follow
it, every time you get one.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` by its absolute path, from
  the working tree you're executing in, and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
If the reviewer reports "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items, read
[references/cannot-verify.md](references/cannot-verify.md) before you mark
the task complete.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

When it triggers, read [references/fix-loop.md](references/fix-loop.md) and
follow it. Read it again before every round, even if you read it earlier in
this session: it holds the round cap, the breaker, and the ledger line each
round writes, and your memory of it does not survive compaction.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

When every task is complete, read
[references/final-review.md](references/final-review.md) and follow it. It
covers the whole-branch review, its single fix wave, and how you finish.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |
| "The implementer spawned its own reviewer — free extra assurance" | It's a duplicate seat reviewing the same diff; the task review is the gate. A worker-spawned reviewer is a defect to flag, not rigor. |
